questions.prompt: What is the intent of the Bridge pattern?

options.text: Decouple an abstraction from its implementation so the two can vary independently
Convert one interface into another
Compose objects into tree structures
Ensure a class has one instance

questions.explanation: Bridge separates two dimensions so each can change independently. Converting interfaces = Adapter; trees = Composite; one instance = Singleton.

questions.prompt: What problem does Bridge primarily prevent?

options.text: The combinatorial explosion of subclasses from combining two dimensions via inheritance
Two threads creating two instances
Shallow copies sharing state
Fat interfaces forcing unused methods

questions.explanation: Combining N shapes with M renderers via inheritance needs N×M subclasses; Bridge makes it N+M across two hierarchies.

questions.prompt: What is the 'bridge' between the two hierarchies?

options.text: A composition link: the abstraction holds and delegates to an implementation interface
A shared base class both inherit from
A global singleton registry
A clone() method

questions.explanation: The abstraction composes an implementor interface and delegates low-level work to it — that link is the bridge.

questions.prompt: How does Bridge differ from Adapter?

options.text: Bridge is designed up front to keep two dimensions independent; Adapter reconciles two existing incompatible interfaces after the fact
They are identical
Bridge only works with third-party code
Adapter always creates families of objects

questions.explanation: Bridge is a planned separation; Adapter is a reactive fix for a mismatch you didn't plan for.

options.text: When there is really only one dimension of change (e.g. a single implementation)
When both the abstraction and implementation grow over time
When you want to swap implementations at runtime
When you have many shapes and many renderers

questions.explanation: With only one implementation there's no second axis to decouple, so the extra interface and delegation add no value.

questions.prompt: Which are genuine benefits of Bridge? Select all that apply.

options.text: Abstraction and implementation can evolve independently
You can switch the implementation at runtime
It guarantees a single global instance
New variants on either side are added without multiplying subclasses

questions.explanation: Bridge gives independent evolution, runtime switching, and linear (not multiplicative) growth. Single-instance guarantees are Singleton's job.
